overview: This two-page Department of State list of papers inventories records numbered 9–27 concerning financial conditions in Japanese-ruled Taiwan during 1930–1939. Most entries concern annual and supplementary budgets of the Taiwan Government-General, but the list also covers a foreign bond issue for the Taiwan Electric Power Company, budget deficits, restrictions on capital flight and foreign exchange, the position of the Yokohama Specie Bank in China, customs interference at Dairen, and an investigation of Taiwan by Japanese bankers. Several entries are cross-references to records filed under Japan, China, Manchuria, and other financial subject headings rather than substantive documents reproduced in this file.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers on financial conditions in Formosa
subfiles.about: An index of Department of State records concerning Taiwan’s budgets, borrowing, banking, exchange controls, and related financial questions from 1930 through 1939.
subfiles.summary: The list describes a sequence of reports from Taihoku on the Taiwan Government-General’s budgets for fiscal years 1930–1931 through 1939, including preliminary estimates, revised and supplementary budgets, and discussion of a deficit. It records the 1931 purchase of $2.8 million in forty-year, 5½-percent gold bonds of the Taiwan Electric Power Company by a banking syndicate that included J. P. Morgan & Company, Kuhn, Loeb & Company, First National Bank, National City Company, and the Yokohama Specie Bank. Other entries point to records on capital-export restrictions, the Yokohama Specie Bank’s difficulties in China, Japanese responsibility for customs interference at Dairen, and a Japanese bankers’ investigation of Taiwan. The second page continues the same numbered inventory begun on the first.

interest: The list is useful as a compact map of State Department reporting on the finances of colonial Taiwan across most of the 1930s, even though the underlying reports are not present here. It reveals both the routine fiscal surveillance performed by the American consular post at Taihoku and the international dimensions of Taiwan’s development financing, particularly the dollar-denominated power-company bond issue involving major American and Japanese banks. The cross-references also show how Taiwan-related financial intelligence became entangled with the Manchurian crisis, Sino-Japanese relations, exchange controls, and Japanese activity at Dairen.
